title: FL: Schools of Hope and Charter Property Grab
author: Peter Greene
summary: Florida's Schools of Hope (2017) was supposed to route charters into neighborhoods served by struggling public schools. The original program stalled because facility costs were prohibitive and facility acquisition takes years. The state responded this year by changing rules rather than retiring the program. Districts must now hand over any underused, vacant, or surplus facilities to Schools of Hope charters with no rent, no lease, no cost, and no ability to refuse, while still providing building maintenance, custodial services, food service, and transportation. Definitions go soft. Fully used means having no unused student seats, which sweeps in intentionally small classrooms serving students with significant needs. A room housing six students, one teacher, and several aides reads as underutilized on spreadsheets while providing essential services. The expansion of SOH eligibility from just low-performing schools to any school with underused space means charters can skip struggling neighborhoods and head for A- and B-rated schools, the market they prefer. Eva Moskowitz's Success Academy is moving into Miami-Dade under the new rules. Operational questions are unresolved: when bell schedules conflict, when cafeteria times do not line up, when public enrollment grows and the district needs space back. The state is silent. Schools of Hope are not subject to the same accountability penalties as public schools, and the state does not collect demographic data for SOH students, so the rescue narrative cannot be tested. The whole move is a double-dip: charter gets state money to operate; public district carries some costs of operating that charter.
points: The program was originally sold as targeting struggling public schools, but the rule change allows charters to skip those neighborhoods and target A- and B-rated schools where markets are stronger.
Definitions of underused space are soft: a classroom with six students and specialized staffing can read as underutilized while providing essential services for students with significant needs.
Districts cannot refuse to hand over facilities, must provide maintenance and support, but charter operators answer to different accountability standards than public schools.
Schools of Hope charters do not submit to the same accountability penalties as public schools, and the state does not collect demographic data, making it impossible to test the rescue narrative.
quotes: The idea was the ultimate in targeting struggling public schools; the idea is that when you find a school that is struggling, you do not give them additional resources or support, but instead pay some charter school to come into the neighborhood.
You are saying funding matters. You are saying good strategies matter. And then you turn around and keep those strategies from schools that you could save from these turnaround options.

Now districts must provide underused, vacant, or surplus facilities to SOH charters. No rent, no lease, no cost, and districts can not refuse. However, the district must provide building maintenance, custodial services, food service, and transportation. And as long as the facilities are underused, the district has no say.

Perhaps on an Excel spreadsheet, a classroom housing six or seven students, one teacher, and several aides may appear to be underutilized, but it is not. It is in fact providing essential services to some of the most vulnerable citizens of our county.

And now that the rules have changed, Schools of Hope no longer target just low-performing schools, but any school with mysterious underused space, many of the schools that are being targeted are A and B rated schools, which is swell for charters, because that's the market they want to tap anyway.
Now charter operators can skip right past those challenging schools and head for the more profitable neighborhoods. Once again, school choice is really school's choice.

A Success rep says this will be great for the public school because the co-located school will get increased state aid because of increased head count in the building. I would not bet on it. Meanwhile, the charter gets to double dip.” Archived from Curmudgucation (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
